commentary.bottom_line: Two post-deployment studies found that subgroup monitoring of deployed tools detected performance differences by age, and hazard studies found that subgroup gaps can emerge or widen after launch. No study tested whether monitoring at set intervals led to correction or better patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: One quasi-experimental study (n=12877) and one cross-sectional study (n=254) tested the practice in real deployments. The first found sensitivity of 70.1% with no subgroup variation, while specificity fell from 93% under age 60 to 84% over age 80 (P<.001). The second found higher positive predictive value under 48 months. Neither measured correction or patient outcomes, so certainty is low.

Hazard studies suggest that subgroup failures can appear after launch. In one, Hispanic/Latino AUC fell from 0.81 to 0.71 in production. In another, race and sex gaps grew over time (P<.01 for trend). A deployed malnutrition model underestimated malnutrition in females. These studies show the problem exists. They do not show that monitoring prevents harm.

The fairness drift study found gaps widening over time after deployment. This suggests that a single validation at launch may miss them and that repeated checks may be needed. The supplied studies do not report monitoring frequency, staff time, or how intervals were matched to tool risk. The proportionate-interval element of this recommendation therefore has no tested basis.

The Canadian study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients and older adults, and the age signal appeared there. The tested and hazard studies stratified by age, sex, and race only. Monitoring designs that omit payer, language, or literacy may miss disparities affecting those groups, and the current evidence cannot say whether they do.

One test was framed as post-market monitoring of a device by sex and age. FUTURE-AI calls for periodic auditing to identify drift and newly occurring biases, and the RUAIH guidance calls for regular monitoring to identify biases. The supplied evidence does not show how such guidance becomes a binding requirement or whether the vendor or the health system holds the monitoring duty.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without scheduled subgroup monitoring, tested which intervals suit which risk tiers, or followed detected disparities through recalibration to patient outcomes. No study measured the staff time or cost of monitoring, and none stratified results by insurance, language, or literacy.
commentary.underserved_note: The Canadian quasi-experimental test focused on racial and ethnic minority patients and older adults. Neither test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether subgroup monitoring detects disparities along payer, language, or literacy lines.
